bib.title: Instruction Tuning for Large Language Models: A Survey

read.skipped: Reference list (about 1,600 lines) skimmed for lineage only; body, tables and the Appendix A dataset table read in full. This is version 10 (6 Oct 2025) of the arXiv paper.

question: What is the state of the literature on instruction tuning (supervised fine-tuning) of LLMs: methodology, datasets, models, modalities, domains, efficient tuning, evaluation, and its role next to RL-based alignment?
contributions: Section 2: general methodology of instruction tuning
Section 3: construction of representative SFT datasets (human-crafted, distillation, self-improvement) and reasoning datasets
Section 5: multi-modality instruction tuning (images, speech, video)
Section 6: domain and application adaptation via SFT
Section 8: evaluation of SFT models, analysis and criticism
Section 9: role of SFT compared with RLHF, DPO, GRPO and prompt engineering

limits: A survey: no experiments of its own, so every number is quoted from the cited works and not re-verified.
Comparisons between models (Section 4) mix human, GPT-4-judged and benchmark scores with different protocols; the survey reports deltas without setups for many.
Authors concede Gupta et al. 2023 did not test large models such as T5-11B and call for larger-scale investigation (Section 8.4).
Section 9 on RLHF/DPO/GRPO is brief and mostly qualitative; no head-to-head numbers.
Several Appendix A table rows carry mismatched citations (for example PRM800K cited as Wang et al. 2022c, O1-Journey as Li et al. 2023g, several reasoning rows as Chen et al. 2024b).
Model coverage is dated to 2023-era open models (Alpaca, Vicuna, LLaMA-1); the reasoning-dataset section (3.4) adds 2024 items but model survey stops before later instruction-tuned families.
practices: Build instruction datasets either by templating existing annotated NLP datasets or by having an LLM generate outputs for manual or seed-expanded instructions (Section 2.1).
For multi-turn data, have an LLM self-play both user and assistant roles seeded with questions (Baize self-chat, Section 3.2).
Train SFT by predicting each output token given instruction and input (Section 2.2).
Prefer small, carefully curated instruction sets when the goal is style and format, per the superficial alignment hypothesis (LIMA, Section 8.5).
Mix several SFT datasets since no single dataset is best across all tasks (Wang et al. 2023e, Section 8.6).
Do not rely on imitating a proprietary model; improve the base model and instruction quality instead (Gudibande et al. 2023, Section 8.7).
Run SFT before RLHF or DPO to establish a base policy; the pipeline is SFT for format and style, then preference refinement (Section 9.1.4).
Use length-controlled or multi-benchmark judging (AlpacaEval LC, MT-Bench, WildBench) instead of raw GPT-4 win rate alone (Section 8.3).
Use parameter-efficient methods (LoRA, QLoRA) or LOMO when full fine-tuning is too memory-expensive (Section 7).
